opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the big idea that Piaget had, and the idea that really has held up, is that children are actively constructing their picture of the world. Before Piaget, there were basically two pictures. There was the empiricist picture, where the child is a kind of blank slate and experience just gets written onto them, and there was the nativist picture, where everything important is already there from the start and just unfolds. What Piaget said was, no, children are like little scientists. They're out there experimenting, they're forming theories, they're revising those theories in the light of evidence, and their knowledge changes in this really deep, structural way as a result.

And that core insight has turned out to be exactly right. When we look at what children are doing, even very young babies, they're not passively absorbing information. They're exploring, they're testing hypotheses, they're paying special attention to things that violate their expectations and then trying to figure out what's going on. That's very much a constructivist picture.

Now, where Piaget was wrong, and wrong in some important ways, was about the details. He thought children were much less competent than they actually are. He thought that babies didn't understand that objects persist when they're out of sight, that young children were egocentric and couldn't take other people's perspectives, that they couldn't reason causally. And it turns out, once we developed better techniques, like looking at where babies look, or designing simpler tasks, we found that even very young children know a great deal more than Piaget thought. He also had this idea of broad, general stages, where everything changes at once, and that hasn't really held up. Development seems to be much more piecemeal, domain by domain.

But what's interesting is that the newer work, especially the work that's come out of thinking about probabilistic models and Bayesian inference, has actually given us a way of making Piaget's constructivism precise. We can now say, computationally, how you could start out with one set of beliefs, get some data, and rationally end up with a quite different set of beliefs. Piaget had these somewhat mysterious notions like assimilation and accommodation and equilibration, and nobody really knew exactly what they meant. Now we have a much better account of how that kind of learning could actually work. So in a funny way, Piaget got the big picture right and the details wrong, and the field has kind of come back around to vindicate the big picture with much better tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing Piaget got deeply right is that children aren't just passively absorbing information, and they aren't just unfolding some innate program either. They're actively constructing theories about the world. If you watch a two-year-old, they're doing something that looks a lot like what scientists do: they have hypotheses, they test them, they revise them when the evidence comes in. Piaget saw that, and he saw it in the 1920s and '30s, with almost no methodology beyond watching his own kids very carefully.

Now, a lot of the specifics didn't hold up. The stages turned out to be much blurrier than he thought. Infants know a great deal more than he gave them credit for. He thought babies didn't understand object permanence until about nine months, and we now know that if you measure it the right way, with looking time rather than reaching, much younger infants have expectations about objects. So the timeline was wrong, and the idea of these neat, discrete stages where everything shifts at once was wrong.

But the core idea, that learning is a process of building and rebuilding representations in response to experience, that's held up remarkably well. And actually, it's held up in a way Piaget couldn't have anticipated, because now we have the formal tools to make it precise. When you look at Bayesian models of cognitive development, or at what's happening in machine learning, you're seeing a version of constructivism with the math filled in. The learner starts with some prior structure, gets data, updates. That's constructivism. Piaget just didn't have the probability theory to say it that way.

The other thing I'd say is that his emphasis on the child as an active explorer, rather than a little adult or a blank slate, has been vindicated by everything we've learned about play and exploration. Children's apparently random, chaotic behavior turns out to be a very effective way of gathering information about the world. So in a sense, he was right about the big picture and wrong about a lot of the details, which honestly is about the best any scientist can hope for.

r003.rationale: It describes learning as building and rebuilding representations in response to experience, with a learner updating after receiving data.

r004.rationale: It presents Bayesian models as a modern, mathematical version of Piagetian constructivism: learners start with prior structure and update it with data.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the central insight is that children aren’t just passively taking in information, and they aren’t simply unfolding a set of things that they already know. They’re actively constructing representations of the world. And they do that by acting on the world, seeing what happens, and changing what they think. That’s a remarkably powerful idea.

One of the things that’s interesting about Piaget is that he got a lot of the particulars wrong. Children know much more than he thought they did, and development doesn’t seem to proceed through the kinds of broad, general stages that he proposed. But the picture of a child as someone who is trying to figure out how the world works, rather like a scientist—that has held up very well.

What we can do now, which Piaget couldn’t really do, is give a more precise account of how that learning might work. How do you get from particular experiences to an abstract understanding of causes? How do you decide what to explore? So I think his enduring contribution is less a particular set of answers than a way of seeing what the problem is: How can interacting with the world produce genuinely new knowledge?

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think Piaget’s really profound insight was that children aren’t just passively taking in information, and they aren’t simply unfolding some set of things that they already know. They’re actively constructing representations of the world, and they’re changing those representations as they encounter new evidence. That basic picture has held up remarkably well, even though many of his particular claims about what children know at particular ages haven’t.

One way of putting it is that he took children’s mistakes seriously. If a child gives you an answer that seems bizarre, you can ask, “What understanding of the world would make that a sensible answer?” That turns out to be an enormously productive way of thinking about development.

What we can do now, which Piaget couldn’t really do, is describe some of those processes computationally. How could a learner start with one picture of how the world works, get evidence, and construct a different picture? And our experiments suggest that even very young children can do much more of that than Piaget thought. So the irony is that correcting his account of children’s limitations has often strengthened his deeper idea about how learning works.

r003.rationale: It says children actively construct representations and change them as they encounter new evidence.
